content: Diethylene glycol (DEG) is an organic compound with the chemical structure HO-CH2-CH2-O-CH2-CH2-OH. It is a clear, odorless, and hygroscopic liquid that can mix completely with water and polar organic solvents, such as alcohols and ethers. Diethylene glycol belongs to a group of compounds known as diols, which are hydrocarbons containing two alcohol groups. These compounds are derived from ethylene oxide and follow the general formula HO-CH2-CH2(-O-CH2-CH2)n-OH. When n = 0, the compound is ethylene glycol, commonly used as antifreeze. When n = 1, the compound is diethylene glycol. When n = 2, the compound is triethylene glycol (TEG), which is a colorless, odorless, and viscous liquid. TEG is used as a plasticizer for vinyl and as a disinfectant when aerosolized in air-sanitizing products. Glycols, including DEG, are also used as liquid desiccants in natural gas processing and air conditioning systems, as well as additives in hydraulic and brake fluids. Higher values of n, such as n = 3 or 4, correspond to tetraethylene glycol and pentaethylene glycol, respectively. For even higher values of n, the resulting compound is polyethylene glycol, a non-toxic polymer. Diethylene glycol has several industrial applications. Like ethylene glycol, it is used in coolant solutions, where it lowers the freezing point and raises the boiling point of the mixture, making it suitable for use in hot climates. DEG is also a precursor in the synthesis of organic compounds such as morpholine and 1,4-dioxane. It serves as a solvent for nitrocellulose, resins, dyes, oils, and other organic substances. Additionally, it acts as a humectant in products like tobacco, cork, printing ink, and glue. DEG is also found in some hydraulic and brake fluids. In personal care products, such as skin creams, lotions, and deodorants, DEG is often replaced by less toxic diethylene glycol ethers. However, DEG has been illegally used as a counterfeit substitute for glycerin in some countries, leading to its inclusion in products like cough syrups and toothpaste. Diethylene glycol is highly toxic to humans and animals. Its ingestion can lead to renal failure and death. Several mass poisonings have occurred due to the substitution of DEG for glycerin, a non-toxic triol (HOCH2CH(OH)CH2OH) commonly used in food and pharmaceuticals. Glycerin is more expensive than DEG, which has led to its illegal use in some cases. Due to its toxicity, DEG is prohibited in food and drug products. In the United States, the Code of Federal Regulations allows no more than 0.2% DEG in polyethylene glycol when the latter is used as a food additive. Notable Mass Poisonings Attributed to Diethylene Glycol: 1. 1937 Elixir Sulfanilamide Disaster (USA): In this infamous case, 107 people died after consuming sulfanilamide dissolved in diethylene glycol. This tragedy led to the enactment of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act of 1938. 2. Haiti (1996): A paracetamol syrup contaminated with DEG caused the deaths of 85 children. The contamination occurred due to the use of glycerin supplied by a Dutch company, which sourced it from a Chinese manufacturer. The exact point of contamination was never determined. 3. Bangladesh (1990): A paracetamol syrup contaminated with DEG caused acute renal failure in 339 children, most of whom died. 4. Panama (2006): A sugarless liquid expectorant containing toxic levels of DEG led to 46 deaths. The contamination was traced to a Chinese company, Taixing Glycerine Factory, which mislabeled DEG as glycerin. The contaminated product was incorporated into 260,000 bottles of cold medicine. 5. Austrian Wine Scandal (1985): Some Austrian wine producers added DEG to their products to enhance sweetness and body. Although the levels were not immediately toxic, the scandal led to a collapse in Austrian wine exports and stricter regulations for wine production. 6. Toothpaste Contamination (2007): Counterfeit toothpaste containing DEG was discovered in Panama, Costa Rica, the United States, and Spain. In Panama, the toothpaste was linked to the same DEG contamination that caused the 2006 cold medicine deaths. The counterfeit products were falsely labeled as originating from reputable manufacturers, such as Colgate-Palmolive, and contained numerous labeling errors. The natural sweetness of diethylene glycol has also led to accidental poisonings in domesticated animals, particularly when they consume antifreeze that has leaked from vehicles.
